question.leadin: This place was originally known as the Flavian Amphitheatre.
question.text: Name this structure which included 80 entrances. Its construction began under the emperor Vespasian [veh-SPAY-zhun] and was completed under the emperor Titus.
question.clue: The construction of a complex tunnel network at this structure, its hypogeum ("hy-PO-jee-um"), ended the prior practice of flooding this place for mock naval battles.

swap.leadin: China wasn't the only country that built great walls.
swap.text: This Roman emperor built a namesake wall to mark the northern boundary of Roman Britain. He also suppressed the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea.
swap.clue: Hebrew sources give him the epitaph "may his bones be crushed" because of his quelling of a revolt supported by Rabbi Akiva, the Bar Kokhba rebellion.

question.leadin: Answer the following about some of Rome's best emperors.
question.text: This second of the group known as "the Five Good Emperors" expanded the Empire to its largest extent and is famous for his namesake column.
question.clue: This man employed Apollodorus of Damascus to build a namesake forum as well as a bridge across the Danube.

swap.leadin: This Master of the Horse under Julius Caesar and member of the Second Triumvirate went to Alexandria in 41 BCE.
swap.text: Name this Roman general and politician, the lover of Cleopatra.
swap.clue: Cicero's head and hands were sent to this leader after Cicero attacked him in his writings and this man was defeated at the Battle of Actium.

question.text: In later Marxist historiography, this rebel leader of the third Servile war became a symbol of ancient class struggle. This former gladiator's troops were crucified en masse following their loss at the Battle of the Silarius River.
question.clue: This Thracian lends his name to a league co-founded by Rosa Luxemburg in 20th-century Germany.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Rome's uneasy dominion over a certain area.
swap.text: In the late 1st century AD, this queen of the Iceni led a revolt against Rome with the help of the close Trinovante tribe. Her uprising would be quelled by Suetonius Paulinus at Watling Street.
swap.clue: This ruler trounced the Ninth Legion but was defeated by Suetonius at the Battle of Watling Street.

question.leadin: Caracalla is presented by many sources as a tyrant, but he wasn't all bad.
question.text: One of Caracalla's great public projects was the construction of his namesake one of the these things, the second-largest in Rome. These places were fed water by aqueducts which was then heated by log fires.
question.clue: Slaves called unctores would often use a strigil on their masters in the destrictarium of these places.

swap.leadin: This war began at Saguntum in Iberia, and after its end Cato the Elder insisted that the losing side had to be fully destroyed in every speech.
swap.text: Name this war which included a disastrous "double envelopment" on one side's home soil at Cannae. A certain Publius Cornelius Scipio got his nickname for ending this war.
swap.answerHtml: Second Punic War [prompt “Punic War” or “Punic Wars” alone; prompt “Carthaginian War”]
swap.clue: This war began with an attack on the city of Saguntum, and its eventual victors suffered terrible defeats at Trebia and Lake Trasimene.

question.leadin: Name these women who bedeviled the Roman Empire.
question.text: When this woman's husband Prasutagus died, Rome annexed his former kingdom, prompting this queen of the Iceni to lead a revolt in East Anglia that was put down by Paulinus.
question.clue: This person's popularity as a patriotic symbol in Victorian Britain was influenced by the theory that her name comes from a root meaning "victory" in Celtic.

swap.text: Androgynous priests known as Galli facilitated the worship of this Roman cult deity. Priests bathed in bull's blood to honor this mother goddess, whose cult became popular during the Second Punic War.

question.leadin: Identify these things related to the early days of Rome.
question.text: The revolt that resulted in Tarquinius' deposition was sparked by his son's rape of this woman.
question.clue: After that, a man threatened to place the naked corpse of a slave next to this woman's bed to frame her for adultery.

swap.text: St Isidore aided in the conversion of Visigothic Spain to Catholicism. The Visigoths had earlier followed this doctrine, which asserted that the Son was subordinate to the Father, and which was condemned at the Council of Nicaea.
swap.clue: The emperor Constantius espoused this belief, leading to its further condemnation at the First Council of Constantinople.

question.leadin: Name some members of Wikipedia's illustrious list of sexually active popes.
question.text: A scene in the Book of Matthew describes Jesus healing this man's mother-in-law, clearly implying that he is married. This man is traditionally considered the first pope.
question.clue: Piux IX installed a statue of this first pope in his namesake basilica in the Vatican. As an apostle this man denied Jesus three times.

swap.text: Before fleeing to the Balearics, Mago was defeated at this battle near Seville by a concealed force of Romans under Scipio Africanus. The battle of Baecula and this battle ended Carthaginian power in Spain.
swap.clue: This battle's victor unusually placed legions on the wings and auxiliaries in the centre, later creating a concave formation that mirrored a battle occurring ten years prior.

question.text: The Senate perception of Maximinus's barbarism was partly inspired by his Carpi ancestry from this region. Aurelian abandoned this region whose past leaders, like Decebalus, fought wars against Trajan and Domitian.
question.clue: Soldiers of this region used the sickle-like falx during a war in which a bridge near the Iron Gates was built by Apollodorus.

swap.leadin: Tarquin the Proud refused to buy these documents at first, leading 6 of them to be burnt.
swap.text: Name these documents written in hexameter that were stored in the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus and guarded by the Decemviri Sacris Faciundis. The general Flavius Stilicho supposedly ordered that they be destroyed.

question.leadin: This man lost an eye while serving in Gaul as a quaestor responsible for recruiting troops for the Social War.
question.text: Name this Roman general who went rogue in the 70s CE and assumed personal rule of several western Roman provinces before Quintus Metellus and Pompey marched against him, inspiring his confederate Vento to assassinate him.
question.clue: Along with his lieutenant Hirtuleius, he overthrew the governor Quintus Metellus Pius, and then was joined by Marcus Perpenna, though Perpenna eventually had this man murdered at a banquet.

swap.text: When Rome first conquered Lusitania, there was an anti-Roman rebellion led by this man. Livy started the tradition that this man was a shepherd, which is how he is portrayed in the Lusiads.
swap.clue: This former shepherd and leader of the Lusitani rose up against Roman control after a governor dug a trench around a group of Lusitani and killed them while they were surrendering their weapons. This leader defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Mt. Veneris.

question.leadin: Identify the following about monumental columns.
question.text: Mainz was home to a classical column dedicated in honor of Nero to this aspect of the chief god of the Roman state, whose official worship took place at his temple on the Capitoline. The Mainz column was a model for other columns erected to worship this god elsewhere in northern Europe.

swap.leadin: Name the following people from early Roman history who may or may not have ever really existed, 5-10-20-30.
swap.text: This king of Clusium led an Etruscan army that attempted to restore the Tarquin monarchy and was eventually beaten by an alliance of Latin cities.
swap.clue: This figure was saved from death when a would-be assassin mistook his scribe for him, and that assassin thrust his right hand into a fire in an act of defiance against this figure.
